summary:
Somalia criminalises same-sex sexual activity, and the sources give irreconcilable penalties. The Human Dignity Trust country profile records a maximum of life imprisonment under a penal code it dates to 1964, together with the death penalty under sharia in some regions. The US State Department's 2021 human rights report gives up to three years, and its 2022 report gives three months to three years for 'carnal intercourse with a person of the same sex'. Article 409 of the penal code, dated by Wikipedia to 1973, carries three months to three years for intercourse and two months to two years for an 'act of lust' other than intercourse; Article 410 permits an additional security measure, usually police surveillance, intended to prevent re-offending.

Under local interpretations of sharia, same-sex conduct is punishable by death. In areas controlled by al-Shabaab and in Jubaland, capital punishment is imposed for consensual same-sex sexual activity at a judge's discretion. The 2022 State Department report records no known state-conducted executions of that kind, and the archived 2010 report noted the death penalty under Islamic law in areas under insurgent control.

Enforcement by the federal authorities is undocumented. The 2022 State Department report states that no official reports of enforcement were available and that impunity generally remained the norm. Wikipedia records that in government-controlled areas civil law provides for up to three years and that LGBTQ people are regularly prosecuted. The two accounts cannot be reconciled from the sources.

ILGA reported killings of people accused of homosexual activity by al-Shabaab or other non-state armed groups: two male teenagers aged 15 and 18 together with a man aged 20 in 2017, a young man in 2018, and two men executed by al-Shabaab in 2024. The inventory supplies no denominator or background homicide rate, so these counts cannot be compared with the general level of lethal violence in the country.

The law does not prohibit discrimination based on sexual orientation or gender identity, as reported by the US Department of State in 2022.

The Marriage Law of 1974 defines marriage as a contract between a man and a woman having equal rights and duties with the object of creating a family, which excludes same-sex unions from legal recognition. A trans visitor whose relationship would be read as same-sex under local law has no route to recognition.

Pervasive social stigma attaches to same-sex relationships, and sexual orientation is a taboo subject with no public discussion in any region of the country, per US State Department reports from 2010 and 2022. Severe societal stigma prevents LGBTQI+ individuals from making their sexual orientation or gender identity known publicly as of 2022. For a visitor, visible gender nonconformity or a disclosed identity carries outing risk.

The 2016 report by Benjamin Christman, reported by Erasing 76 Crimes, found evidence that gay persons should not be returned to Somalia because of persecution risk, supporting refugee-status claims and forming a non-refoulement basis for LGBT asylum seekers.
tangentialFactors:
Al Jazeera reported in July 2013 that gay Somali refugees in Kenya faced death threats and racist discrimination. Al-Shabaab publicised its intent to enforce harsh punishments against homosexuality, and senior figures in the group claimed a death chamber for gay and lesbian people if returned, while UN officials nevertheless pushed return. Persecution drove displacement.

The 2022 State Department report places stigmatisation and criminalisation in a context where 99 per cent of the population follows Islam, amid decades of civil war and unstable government. The 2021 report notes pervasive violence alongside the criminalisation of same-sex conduct.

Family planning services and fact-based information on human sexuality are hard to access, and Islamic social mores often make it difficult to discuss HIV transmission publicly. Since 1999 much AIDS and HIV education and care has come from international organisations such as the United Nations.
localsOnly:
The 2021 State Department report notes statelessness alongside pervasive violence, and the 2022 report states that impunity generally remained the norm.

Human rights and LGBTQ activists, and people accused of homosexuality, have been forced to flee the country for fear of execution or assassination.

As of 2004 one group reportedly existed for LGBTQ people in Somalia. By 2022 there were few, very discreet, mostly online-based LGBTQI+ organisations holding events.
